meta.title: Who really said “Common Sense Is Nothing More Than a Deposit of Prejudices Laid Down in the Mind Before Age Eighteen”? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The words are Lincoln Barnett’s, written in 1948 to describe Einstein’s view — not in quotation marks. Later writers turned the paraphrase into a quotation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said ‘Common Sense Is Nothing More Than a Deposit of Prejudices Laid Down in the Mind Before Age Eighteen’?
meta.ogDescription: Not a quotation. Lincoln Barnett wrote this in Harper’s in 1948 as his own summary of Einstein’s position.

answer.label: Not Einstein’s words — Lincoln Barnett’s paraphrase of him
answer.authorDates: 1909–1979 · American journalist, former editor at Life
answer.sourceLine: This sentence first appears in Lincoln Barnett’s Harper’s Magazine series of 1948, in Barnett’s own voice: ‘as Einstein has pointed out, common sense is actually nothing more than a deposit of prejudices laid down in the mind prior to the age of eighteen’. There are no quotation marks around it — Barnett was summarising a view he understood Einstein to hold, not transcribing him. Later writers added the quotation marks.

source.heading: Where the wording comes from

docMeta.dd: The Universe and Dr. Einstein: Part II

source.excerpt: But as Einstein has pointed out, common sense is actually nothing more than a deposit of prejudices laid down in the mind prior to the age of eighteen. Every new idea one encounters in later years must combat this accretion of “self-evident” concepts.
trail: Quote Investigator locates the earliest relevant text in Lincoln Barnett’s ‘The Universe and Dr. Einstein: Part II’, Harper’s Magazine, May 1948, and notes that Barnett did not place the words between quotation marks. Read the investigation ↗

Quote Investigator records that the earliest instance in quotation marks is later: E. T. Bell’s Mathematics: Queen and Servant of Science (1951) quotes it as ‘Einstein’s remark’. The quotation marks were added by someone other than Einstein. The 1951 citation ↗

Quote Investigator notes that Princeton’s The Ultimate Quotable Einstein (2010) carries a compact version of the saying but that its editor was unable to find any supporting citation. QI on the Calaprice entry ↗

The complicating fact, which Quote Investigator is careful to state: Einstein wrote the foreword to Barnett’s book and praised it, so he had read a text containing this characterisation and apparently did not object to it. QI’s conclusion ↗

author.name: Lincoln Barnett
author.heading: About Lincoln Barnett
author.metaLine: 1909–1979 · American journalist, editor and science writer
author.bio: Lincoln Kinnear Barnett was an American editor and author who worked at Life magazine and became one of the mid-century’s most effective popularisers of science. His three-part Harper’s series of 1948 on relativity, expanded into the book The Universe and Dr. Einstein, carried a foreword by Einstein. One of Barnett’s own sentences from it has been quoted as Einstein’s ever since.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Nobody fabricated this one. A journalist’s summary of Einstein’s thinking slowly hardened into a sentence Einstein supposedly spoke.

items.why: No text has been found in which Einstein says or writes this. Princeton’s The Ultimate Quotable Einstein includes a short form of it, and its editor could find no supporting citation. Quote Investigator ↗
In Harper’s Magazine, May 1948, describing Einstein’s outlook in his own words and without quotation marks. The 1948 citation ↗

items.who: Einstein read the book — and endorsed it
items.why: Einstein contributed a foreword to Barnett’s The Universe and Dr. Einstein, calling it a valuable contribution in which the main ideas of relativity are extremely well presented. Quote Investigator treats this as some evidence the sentiment genuinely accorded with his beliefs, even though the sentence is not his. QI on the foreword ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The idea may well be Einstein’s. The sentence is Lincoln Barnett’s. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Barnett was writing to explain relativity to Harper’s readers, and he needed to account for why the theory feels so wrong. His answer was that intuition is not a faculty but a sediment — a set of assumptions laid down early and defended ever after. It is a good sentence, and it did its job so well that it escaped the article.

This is one of the gentler ways a quotation goes wrong. There is no hoax and no malice: a writer paraphrases, a later writer adds quotation marks, and a reference book records the result. The only casualty is the paraphraser’s name.
context.pull: A writer paraphrases; the next writer adds quotation marks.
